prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated in large numbers, bringing timekeeping to the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single part, B012, with Katori and Ye. Round 1 made the case stronger on the points I care about. Every member who commented agrees that the science is mature and that independent laboratories reproduce the roughly 1e-18 performance, and nobody proposes a different pair or a third name. What persuades me is the record, not the number of supporters. The magic-wavelength lattice is a specific invention. It removes the light shift while keeping thousands of atoms free of Doppler and recoil effects, and it opens a door to things that could not be measured before, such as the gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale sample and clock-to-clock tests of constants. The chair's first question asks what is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes. My answer is that the comb gave the ruler and ion control gave single-system control, but neither covers a many-atom neutral lattice with its magic-wavelength cancellation and the collective systematics that follow. The citation should therefore name the lattice architecture and not metrology in general. On the second question, I would assign the concept and the early strontium demonstrations to Katori and the accuracy, stability and many-body results to Ye, and I would say so in the citation or the accompanying popular text. For the committee's own protection, the 2001 to 2005 priority record (Katori's proposal, Takamoto and Katori's first strontium clock, and the parallel SYRTE work by Lemonde) should be checked against the publications before the final vote. I rely on memory for the dates and the order of the first demonstrations, and that is the single item I cannot be absolutely sure of. On the third question, the redefinition of the second is a decision of the standards bodies and follows the science. It does not validate it, and I now say plainly that the committee should not wait for it. That is a change from my own earlier hesitation.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains lineage and breadth. The 2005 and 2012 prizes cover the neighbouring ground, ion clocks reach comparable uncertainty, and Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Boyd and others contributed to making lattice clocks work. Two names inevitably leave people out. There is also the fair argument from Kroll, Lindroth and Danielsson that this is a measurement technology whose largest fundamental-physics payoffs (varying constants, dark matter, geodesy) are still prospective, so the committee would be rewarding an instrument before the discovery it enables. I think the redshift over millimetres and the agreement between independent clocks are already results about nature, but the point cannot be dismissed. Finally, I have not seen the primary papers during this discussion, so my statements on priority are the weakest part of the case.

responses.point: Mehlig now places B012 above his own opening first choice B057 because of the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang credit gap, and wants the 2001 to 2005 priority record checked before the citation is fixed. He also says my earlier waiting argument conflated a metrology decision with the scientific criterion.
responses.response: You are right on the waiting argument and I have dropped it: the criterion is the demonstrated invention and its verification, not a vote by the standards bodies. I also agree that the priority record from 2001 to 2005 is the one item to verify, and I would add that the check should cover who first demonstrated a lattice clock at the stated accuracy, not only who proposed the magic wavelength. On B057 I agree with your reading and have not changed my view that a Kane, Mele, Molenkamp trio leaves a hole between prediction and measurement. I would put the Z2 idea and the HgTe experiment among the strongest candidates for a later year if the committee can find a fair three-name set.

responses.point: Kroll supports B012 as a clean two-person pairing and discloses his time in John Hall's laboratory, noting that Hall was Ye's doctoral advisor and that he has no joint work or financial interest with Katori or Ye.
responses.response: I take your disclosure at face value. A student-level lineage without joint work or financial interest does not seem to require recusal, but it should be recorded in the minutes, and I would ask that the chair record the same for my own Tokyo connection so that both are visible. On substance, you accept that the 1e-18 and redshift results are Ye's group's, and I propose that the citation wording follow that: the concept, the lattice and the first demonstrations for Katori, and the performance frontier for Ye. I disagree mildly that the ion-clock or ultrastable-laser lineage should be added to the names. Adding either would exceed what the citation can carry within two or three names, and neither is part of the invention being credited.

responses.point: Eriksson keeps B036 first, arguing that the flat-band prediction and the correlated and superconducting states are reproduced and stable even though the pairing mechanism is not, and that eight years of reproduction is not a thin record. He also disputes my treatment of B005, wanting Butler kept in as the symmetry-filtering prediction.
responses.response: Your reproduction argument is fair, and I do not regard B036 as unworthy. It is the one candidate in which an unexpected experimental result changed the field. My difficulty is attribution, not science. The original observation by Jarillo-Herrero's group is clear to me, but the allocation of the theory share between Bistritzer and MacDonald, and the experimental credit relative to Cao, Fatemi and the first authors and to Dean's group, is not something I can be absolutely sure of today. If you can show the committee a record that settles these, I would move B036 up in a later year, and it remains my first alternative. On B005 we still differ. Butler's prediction is important, but Mathon and Umerski made the same prediction independently, and I would credit the experiments of Parkin and Yuasa. I regard B005 as a second alternative only.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps IceCube B029 first, argues that the diffuse flux is robust and that a citation could rest on it alone, and accepts that his own file does not meet my standard of absolute certainty on source associations. He says he would not block B012.
responses.response: I appreciate that you separate the diffuse flux from the source associations, and I agree that the flux is a real discovery. Nothing here changes my reading of the attribution problem. A citation for the diffuse flux alone would rest on a collaboration of hundreds and on the Baikal and AMANDA predecessors, and neither you nor I can say from the record which three people did the decisive original work. I said in round 1 that I could not defend Halzen, Karle and Spiering as the right three without that evidence, and the round has not supplied it. The chair's question to you asks for exactly that evidence. If it is found, I would reconsider B029 in a later year, but I cannot support it this year.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved from IceCube to B012 and argues that the lattice clock is distinct because the comb gave the ruler and ion prize gave single-system control, whereas the lattice combines many atoms with Lamb-Dicke confinement. He also says my first choice B021 has no support beyond me.
responses.response: I accept your description of the distinction and will use it in the draft citation. On B021, you are right that it has no support, and I did not argue it in round 1 because it lies in my own field and I should not drive that discussion. I note one thing for the chair's summary, namely that the priority problem for the STEM corrector, which I raised myself, is real. It is better left for a later year than pressed now. I would ask that the chair's record reflect that my change from B021 to B012 comes from the evidence on attribution and reproduction and not from deference to the opening count.

uncertainties: The exact 2001 to 2005 priority record for the magic-wavelength concept and the first strontium lattice clock demonstrations (Katori, Takamoto, Lemonde, Ye and collaborators). I rely on recollection and the committee should verify it from the publications.

Whether the committee will see the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes when it is worded narrowly around the neutral-atom lattice, and whether the ion-clock and ultrastable-laser communities will feel excluded.

Whether the fundamental-physics payoffs (varying constants, dark matter, geodesy) that Kroll, Lindroth and Danielsson regard as prospective are enough for those who want a result about nature rather than a measurement capability.
For B036 and B005, whether the theory shares (Bistritzer versus MacDonald; Butler versus Mathon and Umerski) and the wider experimental credit can be settled with the certainty I want.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. I am a Fellow of the University of Tokyo (since 2025), and Katori is affiliated with that university, so I record this connection for B012. My profile shows no collaboration, joint publication or financial interest with Katori or Ye, and I regard this as a disclosure and not a ground for recusal, though I leave that to the chair. Kroll's disclosure about the Hall laboratory lineage is noted and I do not read it as requiring a procedural step beyond recording it. B021 (aberration-corrected electron optics) lies in my own field of electron microscopy, so I do not drive any discussion of it. No other conflict is apparent.
